The dictionary store holds no record file for this source and the lane's source cache holds no copy of it, so the source audit (builder/write-fragments.mjs, evidence about the source and no part of any test) read the routes' own def field: on 967 of 967 routes the def is the headword, a space, the route text and the citation of the glossary in square brackets with its page, column and entry number (axis: routes); the route is the glossary's entry with its headword taken out, so 227 routes open with the comma that followed the headword and 47 are one period (axis: routes). definitions.terms: In every test a character is one UTF-16 unit of the JavaScript string (every route here holds only characters of 16 bits). The text is the whole route text as it stands, the field route of a line of the by-source JSONL, what the checker gives the classifier, and never the field def. Nothing is trimmed unless a test says so. The text before the mark is every character from the start of the text up to, and not including, the mark; the text after the mark is every character after it to the end. A letter is any character the JavaScript test \p{L} with the u flag matches; a Latin letter is one of A to Z or a to z; a Hebrew letter is a character from U+05D0 to U+05EA; a digit is one of 0 to 9; whitespace is what \s matches; a space character is U+0020. The run before the mark is the longest run of characters that are not whitespace ending directly before the mark (empty if the character before it is whitespace or it stands first). The word after the mark is the longest run of characters that are not whitespace beginning after the whitespace, if any, that directly follows the mark (empty at the end of the text); its bare form is that run with one period or comma at its end taken off, if it has one. The letters before the mark are the longest run of letters (any script) ending directly before the mark. What the bracket holds means the characters between that opener and its closer: the template's c.group; its first word is its longest run of characters that are not whitespace from its start. Begins with the string means the string's characters are exactly the first characters. Is one of the strings in a list means is equal to one string of that list, character for character and whole. Every string and every list minds case. A string stands between « and », which are not part of it. The container is the template's: top, paren, bracket. The word after the mark bare of every stop is the word after the mark with every period, comma and semicolon at its end taken off, however many stand there (its bare form takes off one only). The text after the mark opens with a string when, the whitespace directly after the mark taken off, the string's characters are exactly its first characters and the character after them, if there is one, is not a letter. The text contains a string when the string's characters stand together, in order, anywhere in the text. The run before the mark, or the word after the mark, bare of every stop and of its question mark is that run or word with every period, comma and semicolon at its end taken off, however many stand there, and then one question mark at its end taken off, if one stands there.

homonyms.reason: The route text carries no entry number; the glossary's page, column and entry number stand in the def field's citation, which the route drops. Keys with more than one text are the glossary's separate entries under one spelling, which the route text tells apart under none; the count holds senses and homonyms together.

branches.question: Many rows list glosses with commas: selected, special, best, p. 20 [Arabic], p. 68 ד. Of 30 drawn at random from the 151 marks B01 and B02 held, 11 joined two wordings of one sense (portion, lot), 19 two senses (friend, uncle): about two in five, range 22 to 54 percent. Does each such comma divide, so that selected, special and best are three readings? Open, as yet: be worthy, able to; ask, wish, require, with infin. or impf. Outside it: commas beside a page, label, stand-in, prose, note (lord, used of God), ibid., Latin word (exitus, conclusion.) or adverb or particle of the verb before (act foolishly, wickedly), and in a row ending in a note on all its glosses (degree, dignity, often.).
